avg_sat = {p: statistics.mean(x[4] for x in sv_by_plant[p]) if sv_by_plant[p] else None for p in PLANTS}
avg_tim = {p: statistics.mean(x[5] for x in sv_by_plant[p]) if sv_by_plant[p] else None for p in PLANTS}

# ---------------- pillar scores (0-100; higher = stronger consolidation candidacy) ----------------
cmin, cmax = min(cap.values()), max(cap.values())
P1 = {p: 100 * (1 - math.log(cap[p] / cmin) / math.log(cmax / cmin)) for p in PLANTS}

kmin, kmax = min(cpu.values()), max(cpu.values())
P2 = {p: 100 * (cpu[p] - kmin) / (kmax - kmin) for p in PLANTS}

P3 = {p: 100 * min(1.0, same_port_absorber_cap[p] / 1000.0) for p in PLANTS}

lr_min, lr_max = min(lr_vals), max(lr_vals)

nc_min, nc_max = min(nc_vals), max(nc_vals)
dt_vals = [detr[p] for p in covered]
dt_min, dt_max = min(dt_vals), max(dt_vals)

def pillar4(p):
    if p not in covered:
        return 50.0  # neutral prior, flagged
    a = 100 * (late_rate[p] - lr_min) / (lr_max - lr_min) if lr_max > lr_min else 0.0
    b = 100 * (n_cmp[p] - nc_min) / (nc_max - nc_min) if nc_max > nc_min else 0.0
    c = 100 * (detr[p] - dt_min) / (dt_max - dt_min) if dt_max > dt_min else 0.0
    return (a + b + c) / 3.0

def lane_cost(orig, w):
    """Average cost to ship w kg from orig->PORT09 across carriers on the lane (AIR)."""
    rows = rates[(rates['Orig_Port'] == orig) & (rates['Mode_DSC'] == 'AIR') &
                 (rates['Min_Weight_Quant'] <= w) & (rates['Max_Weight_Quant'] >= w)]
    if len(rows) == 0:
        return None
    per_carrier = rows.groupby('Carrier').apply(
        lambda g: max(g['Min_Cost'].mean(), g['Rate'].mean() * w), include_groups=False)
    return float(per_carrier.mean())

    """Greedy cheapest-first allocation, joint-closure aware."""

    for cand in CANDIDATES:

        results[cand] = dict(volume_day=vol, ship_day=ship_day, alloc=alloc,

                             unplaced=vol_left, tpt_delta=tpt_new,
                             old_lane=lane_avg[cport], cport=cport)

     "Compare to WhCapacities Daily_Capacity",
     "Figures equal stated daily capacity exactly (1,070 / 11); OrderList cannot validate daily throughput (unit-basis mismatch, single-day extract)", "MISCHARACTERIZED"),
    ("C-5", "Shipments span SEA, AIR and ROAD modes (Sec.1)",
     "Mode coverage in OrderList / FreightRates",
     "OrderList carries no mode field; FreightRates contains only AIR and GROUND; SEA unobservable in any dataset", "NOT VERIFIABLE"),
    ("C-6", "AIR exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs than SEA and ROAD (Sec.2)",
     "Compare slab rates by mode in FreightRates",
     "AIR slab rates $0.048-$18.96/kg; GROUND (only alternative) $12.28-$128.03/kg on 29 rows - blended GROUND rates exceed AIR; claim not supported as stated", "NOT SUPPORTED"),
    ("C-7", "WhCosts contains fixed and variable cost components (Sec.4)",

    ("C-8", "PlantPorts maps plants to port terminals for DTP/CRF routing (Sec.4)",

]

Your first deliverable is a Plant Consolidation Scoring Model (Excel workbook, .xlsx) with four tabs. The \"Composite_Score\" tab should rank all 19 plants on consolidation candidacy using a weighted model with documented weighting rationale. The \"Consolidation_Scenarios\" tab should model volume redistribution for your top closure candidates, accounting for network topology constraints — port access determines which plants can absorb volume from others — and calculating net cost impact. [{"content": "[0] NOVATRANS LOGISTICS
[1] Delivering Excellence Across Every Mile
[3] INTERNAL MEMORANDUM
[5] DATE:  January 15, 2024
[6] TO:  Operations Consulting Team
[7] FROM:  David Chen, Chief Operating Officer, NovaTrans Logistics
[8] SUBJECT:  Engagement Brief: Distribution Network Efficiency Review
[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.
[30] 4. Available Data
[31] The following data exports and reference materials are provided for your analysis. Source files may reflect different operating periods unless otherwise noted:
[33] 5. Expected Deliverables
[34] Upon completion of the engagement, we expect the following deliverables:
[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.
[37] 6. Timeline & Presentation
[38] The deadline for submission of all deliverables is two (2) weeks from the date of this memorandum. Upon submission, the consulting team will be invited to present findings and recommendations to the NovaTrans executive leadership team, including the CEO, CFO, VP of Operations, and VP of Supply Chain.
[39] Please allocate approximately 45 minutes for the presentation, followed by a 15-minute Q&A session. Presentation materials may be prepared in addition to the deliverables listed above, at your discretion.
[40] 7. Points of Contact
[41] For any questions regarding data interpretation, system access, or scope clarifications, please direct inquiries to:
[42] Primary: David Chen, COO -- david.chen@novatrans-logistics.com
[43] Secondary: Maria Santos, Director of Operations -- maria.santos@novatrans-logistics.com

[6] TO:  Operations Consulting Team
[7] FROM:  David Chen, Chief Operating Officer, NovaTrans Logistics
[8] SUBJECT:  Engagement Brief: Distribution Network Efficiency Review
[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.
[30] 4. Available Data
[31] The following data exports and reference materials are provided for your analysis. Source files may reflect different operating periods unless otherwise noted:
[33] 5. Expected Deliverables
[34] Upon completion of the engagement, we expect the following deliverables:
[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.
[37] 6. Timeline & Presentation
[38] The deadline for submission of all deliverables is two (2) weeks from the date of this memorandum. Upon submission, the consulting team will be invited to present findings and recommendations to the NovaTrans executive leadership team, including the CEO, CFO, VP of Operations, and VP of Supply Chain.
[39] Please allocate approximately 45 minutes for the presentation, followed by a 15-minute Q&A session. Presentation materials may be prepared in addition to the deliverables listed above, at your discretion.

Excellent — very useful. Lane cost insights:
- PORT08→PORT09 is dramatically expensive: avg $100.46/shipment vs PORT04 $16.06. So moving PLANT15's volume OFF PORT08 to a cheaper lane saves a LOT of freight per shipment (e.g., to PORT04: save ~$84/shipment; to PORT11: save ~$84).
- PORT09→PORT09 avg $23.58 (intra-port).
- PORT10→PORT09 avg $36.45 (PLANT17's lane — expensive).
- PORT03→PORT09 $27.30 (PLANT02's lane).
- PORT07→PORT09 $20.15 (PLANT14).

Survey: PLANT09 avg overall 2.50 (worst), 50% detractors; PLANT08 3.12, 50% detractors, timeliness 2.62. PLANT13/16/12/04 healthy.

Now let me finalize the composite model and scenario design. One more check — the survey aggregate above shows PLANT03 n=12 (I earlier counted 13; one row must be duplicated customer but n=12 rows... fine, computed from actual rows).

Wait — earlier I listed PLANT03 survey rows: 4,11,12,13,14,17,20,23,26,28,40,42,44 = 13 rows. The agg says n=12. Let me not worry; script computes from data. Actually row 44: ('CUST-008','PLANT03') — I listed it. Hmm 13 vs 12 — whatever, the script's count is authoritative. Actually wait, I should double check: maybe one of those rows is PLANT12 etc. Doesn't matter — final build will compute directly.

Now design the Scenario tab concretely. Candidates (final ranking from the model — I'll compute in build script): expected top-5: PLANT08, PLANT09, PLANT19, PLANT15, PLANT18.

Scenario modeling per candidate:
- Candidate daily volume = Daily_Capacity (units/day proxy per memo framing). 
- Shipments/day = daily volume / median units per shipment (477) — hmm, for tiny volumes: PLANT19 7 units/day → 0.0147 shipments/day → 5.4 shipments/yr. OK.
- For PLANT08: 14 units/day → same formula. But PLANT08 has observed 102 orders (277,008 units) in the extract. The scenario should use capacity basis for consistency; I'll add a column "Observed daily order flow (extract)" as context and a reconciliation note about unit-basis mismatch.

Absorber selection (topology-constrained, greedy cheapest-handling-cost first, respecting joint closure of other candidates):
- PLANT08 (PORT04, CPU 0.5229): same-port absorbers excluding other candidates (09, 19): PLANT03 (1013, 0.5175), PLANT11 (332, 0.5552), PLANT12 (209, 0.7731), PLANT13 (490, 0.4697). Cheapest: PLANT13 (0.4697), then PLANT03 (0.5175), PLANT11 (0.5552), PLANT12 (0.7731).
  Headroom assumption: absorbers at 85% utilization → headroom = 15% of capacity. PLANT13 headroom 73.5 units/day ≥ 14 needed. All 14 units to PLANT13. Handling delta = (0.4697−0.5229)×14 = −$0.74/day (saving). Freight delta 0 (same port). TPT delta 0.
- PLANT09 (PORT04, CPU 0.4651): absorbers: PLANT03 (0.5175), 11 (0.5552), 12 (0.7731), 13 (0.4697) — excluding 08, 19. Cheapest PLANT13 (0.4697) headroom 73.5 ≥ 11 → all to PLANT13. Handling delta = (0.4697−0.4651)×11 = +$0.05/day (tiny increase). 
  But wait — if PLANT08 and PLANT09 both close, their combined 25 units/day both go to PLANT13 (headroom 73.5 covers 25). OK.
- PLANT19 (PORT04, CPU 0.6398): absorbers: PLANT03, 11, 12, 13 → PLANT13 (0.4697) headroom 73.5 ≥ 7 → all to PLANT13. Handling delta = (0.4697−0.6398)×7 = −$1.19/day saving.
- PLANT15 (PORT08, CPU 1.4151, 11 units/day): no same-port absorber. Cross-port absorbers ranked by total landed delta = handling delta + freight delta per shipment × shipments. Candidate absorbers: PLANT13 (PORT07? no — PLANT13 is PORT04)... all plants at other ports: PORT04 cluster (03,11,12,13 + 08/09 if not closed), PORT01/02 (01,07,10), PORT05 (04), PORT06 (05,06), PORT07 (14), PORT09 (16), PORT10 (17), PORT11 (18).
  Landed delta per unit moved to absorber A: (CPU_A − 1.4151) × 1 + (lane_cost(A.port) − lane_cost(PORT08)) / median_units_per_shipment... careful: freight delta applies per shipment; convert to per-unit: shipments/day = 11/477 = 0.0231 shipments/day; freight delta per shipment = lane_cost(A.port→PORT09) − 100.459. For PORT04: 16.064 − 100.459 = −84.40/shipment → ×0.0231 = −$1.95/day. Handling: PLANT13 0.4697−1.4151 = −0.9454×11 = −$10.40/day. Total for PLANT13: −$12.35/day. 
  For PORT09 (PLANT16, CPU 1.9198): freight delta = 23.577−100.459 = −76.88 → ×0.0231 = −1.776; handling (1.9198−1.4151)×11 = +5.55/day → net +3.77/day (worse).
  Best: PLANT13 (PORT04). Also TPT: PORT04 lane TPT ~1.4-3.875 days vs PORT08 TPT 2-14 days (avg ~5.33?) — service improves.
- PLANT18 (PORT11, CPU 2.0363, 111 units/day): cross-port. Shipments/day = 111/477 = 0.2327. Best absorber by landed cost: PLANT13 (PORT04): freight delta 16.064−16.014 = +0.05/shipment ≈ 0; handling (0.4697−2.0363)×111 = −$173.89/day. Huge variable saving. PLANT03 (PORT04, 0.5175): −$168.6/day. But headroom: PLANT13 15% = 73.5 < 111 → PLANT13 alone can't take all; spill to PLANT03 (headroom 152) → 73.5 to P13 + 37.5 to P03. Both PORT04 — fine.
  Hmm wait — why would PLANT18 (111 units/day, $2.04/unit) be closed? Variable savings ~$174/day = $63K/yr. That's the model's outcome; fixed savings would add more. It's the 5th-ranked candidate. OK.

Joint-closure allocation: candidates closing together: 08 (14), 09 (11), 19 (7), 15 (11), 18 (111). Same-port absorbers for the PORT04 trio: PLANT03, 11, 12, 13 (excluding closing 08, 09, 19). Greedy cheapest-first with headroom caps (15% of capacity):
- Headroom: P13 73.5, P03 152.0, P11 49.8, P12 31.4. Total same-port headroom 306.6 ≥ 32 needed (08+09+19). 
- Cheapest-first across the trio: PLANT13 (0.4697) takes 73.5 of the 32 needed... wait total needed is only 32 units/day (14+11+7). PLANT13 headroom 73.5 > 32 → all 32 to PLANT13. 
- PLANT15 (11): cross-port → cheapest landed: PLANT13 but headroom exhausted by trio? 73.5−32 = 41.5 remaining ≥ 11 → PLANT13 takes PLANT15 too (landed delta −12.35/day).
- PLANT18 (111): PLANT13 remaining headroom 41.5−11 = 30.5 → P13 takes 30.5, spill 80.5 to next cheapest: PLANT03 (0.5175, headroom 152): handling delta (0.5175−2.0363) = −1.5188×80.5 = −$122.26/day; freight PORT04 vs PORT11 delta ≈ +0.05/shipment×(80.5/477=0.169 shipments/day) ≈ +$0.008/day. 
  Total PLANT18: P13 part: (0.4697−2.0363)×30.5 = −47.78; P03 part: −122.26. Total ≈ −$170/day.

These numbers are all daily; annualize ×365. Also note this assumes absorbers run at 85% — document. And an alternative utilization assumption (75%) changes headroom. I'll add sensitivity note.

Fixed cost savings: not derivable from data (WhCosts lacks fixed component — reconciliation finding). Parameterize: Low $150K, High $400K per closed site annually (illustrative benchmark, flagged). Transition one-time: $100K–$250K per site. These are clearly-labeled assumptions pending finance validation — the honest approach.

Net cost impact table per candidate:
- Annual variable handling delta (data-derived)
- Annual freight delta (data-derived; 0 for same-port)
- Annual fixed savings (assumption range)
- One-time transition (assumption range)
- Year-1 net (low/high), steady-state net (low/high)
- TPT/service impact

Also allocation detail rows per candidate→absorber: units/day, absorber port, same/cross port, CPU delta, freight delta.

Risk_Matrix tab design:
Rows per candidate plant with:
- Complaint count, severity-weighted count (High=3, Medium=2, Low=1), open/pending count
- Complaint categories
- Survey n, avg overall, avg timeliness, detractor %, representative verbatim comments
- Late-shipment exposure (orders late, late %) where covered
- Customers affected: distinct customers in OrderList for covered plants; "unknown" flag otherwise
- Attrition Risk Rating: PLANT08 High (17.6% late, 50% detractors, 3 complaints incl 1 High), PLANT09 High (50% detractors, avg 2.50, 4 complaints), PLANT19 n/a-unknown (no data — Medium by default with data-gap flag), PLANT15 unknown, PLANT18 unknown.
- Mitigation actions per candidate.

Also a customer-level detail block: complaint rows for candidate plants (from Complaint_Log) — 18 rows with plant, customer, category, severity, status, root cause.

And network-level attrition exposure: survey customers at candidate plants: PLANT08 8 responses (4 detractors), PLANT09 8 (4), plus complaint customers. Named customer IDs (CUST-xxx) at risk: for PLANT08: CUST-026, CUST-011, CUST-007, CUST-027 (complaints) + survey detractors CUST-026, CUST-011, CUST-007, CUST-027... interesting overlap! PLANT09: CUST-030, CUST-034, CUST-025, CUST-021 (survey detractors) + complaint customers CUST-016, CUST-021, CUST-009? no C-004 is PLANT09 CUST-016, C-009 PLANT09 CUST-021, C-014 PLANT09 CUST-016.

Composite_Score tab: 19 rows × columns: Plant, Port(s), Same_Port_Absorber_Cap, Daily_Capacity, Cost_Per_Unit, Coverage flags, P1..P5 scores, Weighted composite, Rank, Data_Coverage flag, plus a weights & rationale block. Use live Excel formulas for the weighted composite (weights in cells so board can tweak).

- Claim verification table (~10 claims)

[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.

import pandas as pd, statistics
from collections import defaultdict
fr = pd.read_csv('/work/task_folder/references/FreightRates.csv')

weights = ol['Weight'].values

    rows = fr[(fr['Orig_Port']==orig)&(fr['Mode_DSC']=='AIR')&(fr['Min_Weight_Quant']<=w)&(fr['Max_Weight_Quant']>=w)]

# per-kg equivalents

[1] Delivering Excellence Across Every Mile
[3] INTERNAL MEMORANDUM
[5] DATE:  January 15, 2024
[6] TO:  Operations Consulting Team
[7] FROM:  David Chen, Chief Operating Officer, NovaTrans Logistics
[8] SUBJECT:  Engagement Brief: Distribution Network Efficiency Review
[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.
[30] 4. Available Data
[31] The following data exports and reference materials are provided for your analysis. Source files may reflect different operating periods unless otherwise noted:
[33] 5. Expected Deliverables
[34] Upon completion of the engagement, we expect the following deliverables:
[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.

[38] The deadline for submission of all deliverables is two (2) weeks from the date of this memorandum. [1] Delivering Excellence Across Every Mile
[3] INTERNAL MEMORANDUM
[5] DATE:  January 15, 2024
[6] TO:  Operations Consulting Team
[7] FROM:  David Chen, Chief Operating Officer, NovaTrans Logistics
[8] SUBJECT:  Engagement Brief: Distribution Network Efficiency Review
[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.
[30] 4. Available Data
[31] The following data exports and reference materials are provided for your analysis. Source files may reflect different operating periods unless otherwise noted:
[33] 5. Expected Deliverables
[34] Upon completion of the engagement, we expect the following deliverables:
[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.
[37] 6. Timeline & Presentation
[38] The deadline for submission of all deliverables is two (2) weeks from the date of this memorandum. Upon submission, the consulting team will be invited to present findings and recommendations to the NovaTrans executive leadership team, including the CEO, CFO, VP of Operations, and VP of Supply Chain.
[39] Please allocate approximately 45 minutes for the presentation, followed by a 15-minute Q&A session. Presentation materials may be prepared in addition to the deliverables listed above, at your discretion.
[40] 7. Points of Contact
[41] For any questions regarding data interpretation, system access, or scope clarifications, please direct inquiries to:
[42] Primary: David Chen, COO -- david.chen@novatrans-logistics.com
[43] Secondary: Maria Santos, Director of Operations -- maria.santos@novatrans-logistics.com
[44] Data/IT: James Park, Senior Data Analyst -- james.park@novatrans-logistics.com
[47] We look forward to a productive engagement and anticipate that your analysis will provide the data-driven foundation needed to optimize our distribution network and strengthen our competitive position.
[49] Regards,
[51] David Chen
[52] Chief Operating Officer

Excellent. Key reconciliation findings confirmed:
1. Orig_Port ↔ PlantPorts mapping: fully consistent ✓
2. Carrier V44_3 in orders but NOT in rate cards (7 rate carriers unused in orders)
3. No customer ID overlap (OrderList V55555_x vs survey CUST-xxx)
4. Late shipments concentrated: PLANT03 (174) + PLANT08 (18) = 100%; DTP service (183) and carrier V444_0 (183)
5. Single-day order file (5/26/13)
6. AIR vs GROUND: GROUND avg rate much higher but only 29 rows; memo claim about AIR higher than SEA/ROAD — SEA absent entirely; GROUND limited.

Rate structure: most lanes are AIR with weight-slab pricing; PORT09→PORT09 (intra-port) has cheap rates (~0.048/kg at bulk slab). This matters for PLANT16 — moving PLANT15's volume to PLANT16 (PORT09) means the lane becomes PORT09→PORT09.

For scenario freight costing, I'll use the bulk slab (2000-99999.99 kg) representative rate per lane... but median order weight is only 4.44 kg, which falls in slab 4-4.99 or similar small slabs with much higher rates (1.8272 for 10-14.99). Let me look at the full slab structure per lane to model properly. Actually a cleaner approach for the scenario tab: compute a **per-kg blended rate** for each lane using the OrderList weight distribution (apply each lane's slab rates to the actual observed weight distribution of orders, computing average cost per kg and cost per shipment including Min_Cost floor).

That's a defensible methodology: "Lane cost model: apply each lane's weight-slab rate card to the observed shipment weight distribution from OrderList (median 4.44 kg), deriving average cost per shipment and per kg; freight delta for cross-port moves = new-lane minus old-lane average cost per shipment."

Let me build that: for each lane (orig port), for each carrier+service in that lane, compute cost(w) = max(Min_Cost, Rate(w_slab) × w) for the observed weights, average across orders. Then delta per shipment for candidate→absorber moves.

But careful: which carrier? Orders use V444_0, V444_1, V44_3. Rate cards have V444_0..9 (no V44_3). For lane costing use the carrier present in orders on that lane if available, else average across carriers on the lane. PLANT03 orders use V444_0/V444_1 presumably. Let me check carrier by plant/port.

Also TPT (transit time) — service continuity: new lane TPT vs old lane TPT. Include TPT delta in scenario (service impact).

Now, what about DTP vs DTD vs CRF — rates exist for DTD/DTP in the cards (CRF missing from rate cards? let me check service levels in rates: DTD, DTP only — CRF has no rate card! Another reconciliation finding: CRF orders (854, all V44_3 presumably) have no rate coverage. Actually all CRF orders = 854 = exactly the count carried by V44_3. Let me verify: CRF by carrier.

Let me now also figure out the units question for scenario volumes. The scenario needs a volume base for candidates:
- PLANT08: covered — 102 orders, 277,008 units on the observation day.
- PLANT19, 15, 17, 18: uncovered — use daily capacity (7, 11, 8, 111 units/day) as volume proxy.

Hmm, but wait: PLANT08's observed daily units (277,008) vastly exceed its stated capacity (14/day). So observed flow >> capacity for PLANT08 — weird. PLANT03: 28.6M units vs capacity 1013. So Unit_Quant is clearly not "units handled per day at the plant" — it's cumulative order line quantity (maybe pieces in the order). The memo's throughput claims (1070/day PLANT01, 11/day PLANT15) exactly match capacity values, so the memo treats capacity AS throughput. For scenario modeling I'll use the stated daily capacity as the volume base (documented assumption), and for PLANT08 additionally note observed order flow.

Actually, for consistency and defensibility, use **daily capacity** as the volume proxy for ALL candidates in the scenario model (that's the memo's own throughput framing). The PLANT08 case: 14 units/day capacity — tiny. Its 102 orders/277K units on the extract day conflict with 14/day capacity → flag in reconciliation as internal inconsistency (either capacity file is wrong for PLANT08 or order extract is not a single day / different unit basis). Good finding: "PLANT08 processed 277,008 units across 102 orders in the shipment extract while stating a daily capacity of 14 units — irreconcilable scale mismatch indicating inconsistent unit bases across systems."

Wait, actually PLANT09: 12 orders, 223,830 units vs capacity 11/day. Same pattern. PLANT04: 1 order, 348 units vs cap 554. So the mismatch is systemic, not just PLANT08. The order unit quantities are simply on a different basis (order line quantities, maybe pieces vs pallets). Reconciliation finding: Unit_Quant basis differs from Daily_Capacity basis by ~3-4 orders of magnitude; utilization cannot be computed directly; recommend master-data alignment.

OK so now design the composite model with clean, computable metrics. Let me finalize:

**Composite Score = weighted sum of 5 pillars (0-100 each):**

P1. Scale Deficit — 30%
Metric: Daily capacity (WhCapacities). Small = high candidacy. Normalize: score = 100 × (1 − (cap − min)/(max − min))? That linearizes 7..1070. PLANT19=100, PLANT01=0. But most plants cluster low; log scale better: score = 100 × (1 − (ln(cap)−ln(min))/(ln(max)−ln(min))). Hmm, min-max on ln: PLANT19 (7)=100, PLANT17 (8)= 1−ln(8/7)/ln(1070/7)=1−0.1335/5.0346=97.3, PLANT15 (11)= 1−ln(11/7)/5.0346=91.1, PLANT08 (14)=88.2, PLANT06(49)=61.6, PLANT18(111)=48.0, PLANT02(138)=44.3, PLANT12(209)=36.6, PLANT11(332)=27.6, PLANT07(265)=31.4, PLANT05(385)=23.0, PLANT13(490)=17.6, PLANT16(457)=18.8, PLANT14(549)=14.9, PLANT04(554)=14.7, PLANT10(118)=44.6... wait ln(118/7)=2.833/5.0346 → 1−0.5628=43.7. PLANT09(11)=91.1 (same as 15), PLANT03(1013)=6.2, PLANT01(1070)=0.
Rationale: sub-scale facilities cannot absorb fixed operating overhead; the smallest quartile is structurally unviable as standalone units.

P2. Unit-Cost Disadvantage — 25%
Metric: WhCosts Cost_Per_Unit. score = 100 × percentile-rank (higher cost → higher). Linear min-max: min 0.3714 (P07)=0, max 2.0363 (P18)=100.
PLANT18=100, PLANT16=92.4, PLANT15=61.9, PLANT12=23.8, PLANT19=15.9, PLANT14=15.6, PLANT01=11.6, PLANT11=10.9, PLANT06=10.8, PLANT10=7.2, PLANT08=8.9... compute: (0.5229−0.3714)/(2.0363−0.3714)=0.1515/1.6649=9.1. PLANT03=8.8, PLANT05=7.0, PLANT02=6.4, PLANT09=5.6, PLANT13=5.9, PLANT04=3.4, PLANT17=3.5, PLANT15=(1.4151−0.3714)/1.6649=62.7, PLANT12=(0.7731−0.3714)/1.6649=24.1, PLART19=(0.6398−0.3714)/1.6649=16.1, PLANT14=(0.6343−0.3714)/1.6649=15.8.
Rationale: high variable handling cost per unit erodes margin; volume migrating to cheaper facilities yields direct savings.

P3. Absorption Feasibility (network topology) — 20%
Metric: same-port absorber capacity (sum of other plants' capacity at shared ports). score = 100 × min(1, same_port_cap / 1000). Plants: PORT04 cluster members get 1063→100 (except P03 gets 1063 too as its "absorbers" are 08,09,11,12,13,19=1063). P10: 1335→100, P07: 1188→100, P01: 383→38.3, P06: 385→38.5, P05: 49→4.9, isolated (02,04,14,15,16,17,18): 0.
Hmm — but a zero here just says "harder"; it doesn't mean "don't close" — cross-port absorption possible with freight delta. Keep it as feasibility friction. Rationale: same-port migration preserves port routing for DTP/CRF and avoids re-contracting lanes; isolated plants incur freight deltas and carrier re-contracting.
Hmm, PLANT16 has zero same-port absorber AND high cost AND decent scale — it'll rank mid. Fine.

For covered plants (03,04,08,09,12,13,16): sub-score = mean of:
  (a) late-rate percentile (late orders/total orders of plant, min-max normalized across covered: P03 2.04% → (2.04-0)/(17.65-0)*100=11.6; P08=100; others 0)
  (b) complaints per 100 observed orders? P03: 6/8541=0.07, P08: 3/102=2.94, P09: 4/12=33.3 — tiny denominators explode. Use complaint count percentile instead: P03=6 (max), P09=4, P08=3, P12=2, P13=2, P16=2, P04=1 → min-max → P03=100, P09=60, P08=40, P12/13/16=20, P04=0.

[1] Delivering Excellence Across Every Mile

[5] DATE:  January 15, 2024
[6] TO:  Operations Consulting Team

[8] SUBJECT:  Engagement Brief: Distribution Network Efficiency Review
[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.
[30] 4. Available Data
[31] The following data exports and reference materials are provided for your analysis. Source files may reflect different operating periods unless otherwise noted:
[33] 5. Expected Deliverables
[34] Upon completion of the engagement, we expect the following deliverables:
[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.

[38] The deadline for submission of all deliverables is two (2) weeks from the date of this memorandum. [8] SUBJECT:  Engagement Brief: Distribution Network Efficiency Review
[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.

[33] 5. Expected Deliverables

[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.

FreightRates insights:
- All lanes terminate at PORT09 (matches OrderList Dest_Port=PORT09)
- Modes: AIR and GROUND (memo says SEA/AIR/ROAD — reconciliation finding: rate cards contain only AIR/GROUND; no SEA rates; OrderList has no mode column at all — memo's mode-level claims can only be partially verified)
- 9 carriers, though OrderList only uses 3 (V444_0, V444_1, V44_3 — wait, V44_3 isn't even in FreightRates! Carriers in rates: V444_0..V444_9. V44_3 appears in OrderList but not in rate cards — another reconciliation finding!)

Let me check: OrderList carriers: V444_0, V444_1, V44_3. FreightRates carriers: V444_0, V444_1, V444_2, V444_4, V444_5, V444_6, V444_7, V444_8, V444_9. So V44_3 is unmatched. Also V444_2,4..9 unused in orders.

- Rate comparison AIR vs GROUND: avg AIR rate 2.61 vs GROUND 17.61?? That's odd — GROUND more expensive per-unit? Note Min_Cost GROUND 42.92 vs AIR 11.74. Hmm, but GROUND lanes are only PORT03→PORT09 and PORT09→PORT09. Memo says AIR "exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD" — from the rate cards, AIR avg rate 2.61 < GROUND 17.61. But wait — GROUND has few rows (29), maybe small weight slabs. Need to compare at equivalent weight slabs. Let me check. Actually the memo claim says AIR higher per-unit vs SEA and ROAD. We can't verify SEA at all (no SEA rates exist). For ROAD vs AIR — GROUND presumably maps to ROAD. Compare same weight slabs.

Let me check the GROUND rates detail and AIR rates at low weight slabs. Also check TPT day counts (AIR=2 days per earlier sample).

Also there's PORT09→PORT09 lane (PLANT16 to PORT09 — same port, makes sense since PLANT16 is at PORT09).

Port mapping for rate coverage:
- PORT02 → PLANT01, PLANT07, PLANT10 (also PORT01, but PORT01 has NO rate card!) — reconciliation finding: PLANT01/07/10 list PORT01 & PORT02, but only PORT02 lanes are rated.
- PORT03 → PLANT02
- PORT04 → PLANT03, 08, 09, 11, 12, 13, 19
- PORT05 → PLANT04
- PORT06 → PLANT05, 06
- PORT07 → PLANT14
- PORT08 → PLANT15
- PORT09 → PLANT16
- PORT10 → PLANT17
- PORT11 → PLANT18

All 10 origin ports have AIR lanes to PORT09. Good — every plant's port has an outbound rate to PORT09, enabling cross-port redistribution costing.

Now, the memo also claims "Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume" — can't verify from a single-day order file (no trend data). Reconciliation: not verifiable.

Memo claims to verify:
1. 19 plants ✓ (WhCapacities: 19; PlantPorts: 19; WhCosts: 19)
2. 9,000+ shipments ✓ (9,215 rows)
3. ~2% late ✓ (2.08%)
4. PLANT01 ~1,070 units/day & PLANT15 ~11 units/day — matches WhCapacities (1070/11) exactly; flag that these equal stated capacity not observed throughput.
5. Three service levels CRF/DTD/DTP ✓ present in OrderList (854/2143/6218).
6. Modes SEA/AIR/ROAD — OrderList has no mode field; FreightRates has only AIR/GROUND; SEA not present. Partially verifiable only.
7. AIR higher per-unit cost — compare vs GROUND at matched slabs; SEA unverifiable.
8. Memo Section 4 says WhCosts includes "fixed and variable cost components per plant" — actual file has only Cost_Per_Unit. Reconciliation finding.
9. Memo says PlantPorts is "Mapping of each plant to its associated port terminal(s)" ✓.

Additional cross-checks for Data_Reconciliation:
- Plant coverage matrix across 7 datasets (OrderList, Survey, Complaints, WhCapacities, WhCosts, PlantPorts, FreightRates-via-port).
- OrderList carriers vs FreightRates carriers (V44_3 missing from rate cards).
- Orig_Port vs PlantPorts mapping consistency: PLANT03→PORT04 ✓ matches OrderList Orig_Port PORT04 for PLANT03. PLANT16→PORT09 ✓. PLANT04→PORT05 ✓. All consistent — verify programmatically.
- Dest_Port PORT09 served by PLANT16 (the port's plant) — all orders destined PORT09.
- Date coverage: single day 5/26/13 vs survey Q4 2023 — different operating periods (memo itself notes this).

Now the composite scoring model. Let me define metrics computable for all 19 plants:

A. **Scale Deficit (30%)**: Daily_Capacity. Tiny plants = structurally unviable scale. Score = percentile rank inverted (small capacity → high candidacy). Rationale: fixed-cost absorption; board concern.

B. **Unit-Cost Disadvantage (25%)**: Cost_Per_Unit from WhCosts. High cost → high candidacy. Rationale: consolidation migrates volume to lower-cost facilities.

C. **Absorption Feasibility / Network Redundancy (20%)**: Does the plant share a port with at least one plant having spare capacity? Same-port absorber capacity available. Score high when same-port absorber headroom is large (easy, low-cost migration); isolated single-port plants score low candidacy on this dimension (harder to close without port change) — though cross-port absorption is possible at freight cost. Rationale: topology determines migration cost/risk.

D. **Service Performance Deficit (15%)**: composite of late-shipment rate (OrderList), complaint intensity (complaints per 100 orders or per plant), and survey detractor share for covered plants. For uncovered plants — use neutral prior with coverage flag? Hmm. For uncovered plants we lack data; assigning them neutral (network median) with a flag is defensible. Rationale: underperforming plants strengthen the consolidation case (closes service gap while consolidating).

E. **Observed Flow Displacement (10%)**: For plants covered in OrderList: share of network order flow (tiny share → candidacy). For uncovered plants: unknown → use capacity-based flow proxy (capacity percentile). Hmm, this may double count with A.

Alternative E: **Utilization risk** — can't compute. Let me instead make E = "Demand Coverage Gap (10%)": plants with no observed orders in the shipment extract (12 of 19) get a coverage-adjusted score — no, that penalizes plants for missing data, which conflates data gap with viability. Better to keep E as data-confidence adjuster: score = neutral for uncovered, actual for covered. Actually for the 7 covered: PLANT04 has 1 order (348 units) with capacity 554 — nearly zero flow. PLANT09 12 orders (223,830 units — huge unit quantities! interesting: PLANT09's 12 orders carry 223,830 units vs PLANT03's 8,541 orders carrying 28.6M). Unit_Quant varies wildly.

Hmm, honestly the cleanest defensible composite for a board deliverable:

**Pillar 1 — Structural Scale (35%)**: capacity percentile (small = high candidacy). All 19 plants.
**Pillar 2 — Cost Position (25%)**: unit handling cost percentile (high = high candidacy). All 19.
**Pillar 3 — Network Absorbability (20%)**: same-port absorber headroom (high headroom = high candidacy); cross-port fallback noted. All 19.
**Pillar 4 — Service & Risk Signal (15%)**: late rate + complaints + detractors where covered; network-median prior where not covered, with explicit coverage flag and sensitivity note. 
**Pillar 5 — Observed Flow Viability (5%)**: order flow share for covered plants (near-zero flow = high candidacy); for uncovered plants, neutral 50 with flag.

Weights rationale: Scale is the primary structural viability determinant (sub-scale plants cannot absorb fixed overhead — the board's core concern); cost position quantifies margin drag; absorbability gates feasibility (a plant that cannot be absorbed cheaply is a poor closure candidate regardless of scale); service signals capture customer-impacting underperformance; flow viability is smallest because order data covers only 7 plants on one day (low evidentiary weight, documented).

Let me compute. Capacity percentile (smaller → higher candidacy score, 0-100). Cost percentile (larger → higher). Absorbability: for each plant, sum of (same-port other plants' capacity) → headroom proxy; normalize: high = easy absorption. For isolated plants: 0 same-port headroom → low absorbability score → lower candidacy. Hmm wait — but PLANT15 (11 cap, high cost, isolated) — should it be a candidate? **Customer Satisfaction Survey Q4 2023**:

Key insight for consolidation: the memo's PLANT15 ~11 units/day and PLANT01 ~1,070 units/day claims exactly match WhCapacities capacity figures — so "throughput" in the memo is likely capacity data. The plants with tiny capacity: PLANT17 (8), PLANT19 (7), PLANT15 (11), PLANT08 (14), PLANT06 (49).

For the composite scoring model, I need to define "structurally unviable" and operationalize it with the available data:

Proposed composite scoring dimensions (weighted):
1. **Scale/Viability (Volume & Capacity)** — very small daily capacity relative to network (PLANT19=7, PLANT17=8, PLANT15=11, PLANT08=14 units/day) means structurally unviable scale. Also throughput from OrderList where available.
2. **Cost efficiency** — WhCosts per-unit cost (PLANT16=1.92, PLANT18=2.04 high; PLANT07=0.37, PLANT17=0.43, PLANT04=0.43 low).
3. **Network redundancy / port overlap** — plants sharing the same port can absorb each other's volume (PORT04 cluster: 03,08,09,11,12,13,19; PORT01/02 cluster: 01,07,10; PORT06 cluster: 05,06). Isolated ports (PLANT14→PORT07 only, PLANT15→PORT08, PLANT16→PORT09, PLANT17→PORT10, PLANT18→PORT11, PLANT02→PORT03, PLANT04→PORT05) have no redundancy → consolidation would require port change. This affects consolidation feasibility.
4. **Service quality / customer risk** — complaint counts, late rates, survey satisfaction by plant (only for the 7 active plants).
5. **Utilization** — actual order volume vs capacity for the 7 active plants; for the other 12, no order data (coverage gap → flag in reconciliation).

Wait — important reconciliation point: OrderList only covers 7 plants. So for the other 12 plants, the only data we have is capacity, cost, and port mapping. The scoring model must rely on structural data (capacity, cost, port access) for those, with a data-coverage flag.

Scoring approach:
- Normalize each metric 0–100 or 0–1 across the 19 plants.
- Higher score = stronger consolidation candidacy.

Proposed weights (with rationale):
1. Capacity Scale Deficit (30%) — sub-scale facilities cannot absorb fixed costs; board concern re: structural viability. Metric: daily capacity relative to network median/mean; smallest plants score highest.
2. Unit Cost Disadvantage (25%) — high per-unit handling cost (WhCosts) erodes margin; consolidation moves volume to cheaper plants.

[1] Delivering Excellence Across Every Mile
[3] INTERNAL MEMORANDUM
[5] DATE:  January 15, 2024
[6] TO:  Operations Consulting Team
[7] FROM:  David Chen, Chief Operating Officer, NovaTrans Logistics
[8] SUBJECT:  Engagement Brief: Distribution Network Efficiency Review
[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.
[30] 4. Available Data
[31] The following data exports and reference materials are provided for your analysis. Source files may reflect different operating periods unless otherwise noted:
[33] 5. Expected Deliverables
[34] Upon completion of the engagement, we expect the following deliverables:
[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.
[37] 6. Timeline & Presentation
[38] The deadline for submission of all deliverables is two (2) weeks from the date of this memorandum. Upon submission, the consulting team will be invited to present findings and recommendations to the NovaTrans executive leadership team, including the CEO, CFO, VP of Operations, and VP of Supply Chain.
[39] Please allocate approximately 45 minutes for the presentation, followed by a 15-minute Q&A session. Presentation materials may be prepared in addition to the deliverables listed above, at your discretion.
[40] 7. Points of Contact
[41] For any questions regarding data interpretation, system access, or scope clarifications, please direct inquiries to:
[42] Primary: David Chen, COO -- david.chen@novatrans-logistics.com
[43] Secondary: Maria Santos, Director of Operations -- maria.santos@novatrans-logistics.com
[44] Data/IT: James Park, Senior Data Analyst -- james.park@novatrans-logistics.com
[47] We look forward to a productive engagement and anticipate that your analysis will provide the data-driven foundation needed to optimize our distribution network and strengthen our competitive position.
[49] Regards,
[51] David Chen
[52] Chief Operating Officer
[53] NovaTrans Logistics
